analysis.one_liner: Requires airlines to monitor cabin air for toxic fumes, train crews to respond, and report incidents publicly.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote in the House before Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The Cabin Air Safety Act would have required airlines to install equipment that detects contaminated air in the cabin and alerts the crew, and required pilots, flight attendants, mechanics, and airport responders to be trained annually on handling smoke or fume events. It would also have created a standardized FAA reporting form and a public, searchable database of incidents, and required the FAA to investigate any incident where someone needed medical attention. The bill died in committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Airline passengers and crew, who are routinely exposed to the cabin air that comes off the engines. The bill would give them real-time warnings of contaminated air, annual training for the crews who must respond, and a public record of how often these incidents happen and on which aircraft.

how_it_helps.text: Requires annual training for flight attendants, pilots, maintenance technicians, and airport first responders on recognizing and responding to smoke or fume events.
Creates a standardized reporting system for smoke and fume incidents, with a public, searchable FAA database of events.
Requires an FAA investigation whenever a reported incident involved someone needing medical attention.

Requires airlines to install and operate onboard air-quality monitoring equipment in the air supply system, including carbon monoxide detection, that alerts the pilot and flight attendants to dangerous air quality.

analysis.who_pays: Airlines would pay for onboard air-quality monitoring equipment and annual training; aircraft and engine manufacturers would have to incorporate that equipment into manuals and minimum equipment lists. Some of that cost could reach travelers through fares.

drawbacks.text: The bill places new costs on air carriers: installing continuous air-quality monitoring equipment, annual training for crews and first responders, and incident investigations after any medical attention is required — costs that could ultimately show up in ticket prices.

Mandated detectors and standardized investigation procedures add compliance and maintenance work to aircraft operations, and critics could argue that existing voluntary reporting and engine-reliability record make a statutory system unnecessary.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits — earlier detection of toxic air and better response to an exposure problem that has been documented for decades — are real and the costs are modest: detector hardware, annual training, and paperwork. The main counterargument is that engine oil fume events are relatively rare and modern engines are reliable, so airlines would pay recurring costs for protection against an infrequent hazard. The bill never got a committee hearing, so there is no record weighing those costs against the safety benefit.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and its Aviation Subcommittee, where it stayed without a hearing or vote until Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 1, 2023 by Rep. Garamendi with Rep. Fitzpatrick and referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure.
On March 2, 2023 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Aviation, and no further action was taken.
No markup, committee vote, or House floor vote ever occurred before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
The bill had 54 cosponsors, including 48 House Democrats and 6 House Republicans, but that support never translated into committee action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Airlines avoid the cost of installing cabin air monitoring equipment and annual training, and continue without standardized public reporting of fume incidents.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Airlines, which avoid monitoring and training costs

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was bipartisan but lopsided: 48 Democrats and 6 Republicans signed on, and no vote ever took place so no roll-call record exists.

industries.note: Airlines would bear the cost of installing and maintaining monitoring equipment, training crews annually, and FAA investigations after incidents. In exchange, incidents that today often go unrecorded would be documented and traceable to specific aircraft and engines.

Manufacturers would have to add air-quality monitoring equipment to minimum equipment lists and include alarm-response procedures in aircraft manuals. Public incident data could expose which engine types and oil products are prone to fume events.

industries.industry: Occupational health and cabin-air sensor technology
industries.note: The bill directs continued FAA research into sensors and monitoring techniques, and makes onboard detection a permanent regulatory requirement rather than an optional retrofit.
